title: C-suite Elevation Kit: Inference Economics, Controls, and Pilot Playbook
author: Sofia Ramirez
summary: A compact, executive-focused kit for sellers and AEs to run high-impact conversations with C-level buyers. Includes positioning lines, competitive differentiation, pricing/pilot templates, a compact case study, and a prospect security FAQ tailored for regulated buyers.
content:
Overview:

This page is an actionable kit for running executive-level conversations: economic levers, deployment risk controls, pilot structures, and short security answers that close procurement questions. Use the deck outline for CXO briefings, the pricing scenarios for pilot proposals, and the security FAQ for technical due diligence calls.

1) Executive framing and positioning (30-second and 3-minute variants)

- 30-second elevator for CXOs:
  - Redwood Inference helps engineering teams deploy and scale LLM features with predictable latency, transparent unit economics, and enterprise controls whether you use hosted API, reserved capacity, or a private VPC deployment.

- 3-minute problem-solution pitch for strategic buyers:
  - Problem: Teams are seeing model performance vary by workload and hardware, budgets balloon from token spikes, and legal wants consistent controls across environments.
  - Solution: Redwood unifies serving, routing, and observability so you get a single contract and operational model across hosted and private deployments. We reduce token cost via caching and batching, enforce controls via RBAC and KMS integrations, and keep apps online with automatic fallback policies.

Key executive messages to emphasize (choose 3):
- Predictable economics: per-token and per-embedding unit transparency, with recommendations to reduce cost by 15-40% via caching and quantization profiles.
- Deployment flexibility: same API and controls across hosted, dedicated, and private modes, reducing integration effort and audit surface.
- Reliability guarantees: SLA-backed latency percentiles, automatic fallbacks, and multi-region routing for business continuity.

2) Competitive brief (concise)

- Competitor axes we hear in deals: model access breadth, ease of integration, latency/cost at scale, enterprise controls, and private deployment support.

- Redwood short differentiators by axis:
  - Model access: Curated open models and Redwood-verified performance profiles for common sequence length distributions.
  - Integration: Single API, streaming, function-calls, and structured output with SDKs and templates for quick PLG adoption.
  - Cost/latency: Runtime-level batching, prefix caching, and kernel selection reduce per-token cost without changing model fidelity.
  - Controls: Private control plane option, KMS/HSM integrations, audit logs, and role-based policies.
  - Deployment: Hosted API for rapid pilots, Dedicated for guaranteed throughput, Private for regulated workloads.

- One-page comparison table (text)
  - Columns: Company | Hosted API | Private/VPC | Enterprise SLA | Cost Controls | Observability
  - Redwood | Yes | Yes (private control plane + on-prem) | SLA + dedicated capacity | Batching, KV caching, quant profiles | Token-level tracing, per-route dashboards
  - Controls-focused competitor X | Yes | Limited | Optional | Client-side only | Basic logs
  - Low-cost inference vendor Y | Yes | No | No | Heavy quantization required | Minimal metrics

3) Pricing guidance and pilot templates

Objective: get to a 6-10 week pilot that demonstrates integration effort, latency/cost baselines, quality, and operational controls. Present 2 pilot flavors: API-first and Private-proof.

- API-first pilot (recommended for speed):
  1) Duration: 6 weeks
  2) Scope: 1 production route or product flow (e.g., support chat summarization or recommender reranking) at realistic QPS for that flow
  3) Commitment: Free trial credits up to $10k usage or 4 weeks of hosted capacity, then negotiated monthly commit if proceeding
  4) Deliverables: integration checklist, baseline latency and cost report, quality checks on 5 core prompts, go/no-go decision checklist

- Private-proof pilot (recommended for regulated customers):
  1) Duration: 8-10 weeks
  2) Scope: Private control plane, sample dataset ingestion (synthetic or redacted), 1-2 model variants, smoke tests for KMS and audit logging
  3) Commitment: professional services estimate + temporary reserved capacity credits, sample SOC artifacts shared under NDA
  4) Deliverables: onboarding runbook, security evidence packet, performance baseline, and handoff plan to ops

Pricing anchors for pilots (example scenarios):
- Small pilot: $0 setup (self-serve), $10k trial credits, partner enablement hours (8 hrs) included
- Medium pilot with Private proof: $20k professional services deposit (applied to contract), $25k-50k temporary reserved capacity depending on footprint
- Enterprise commitment guidance: typical Dedicated deals start at $100k/month reserved capacity with multi-month/year discounts and add-on fees for extended observability retention or premium SLA

4) Sample pitch deck outline and speaker notes

- Slide 1: Title + Hook
  - Note: 1-line customer problem statement, 1-line Redwood value proposition
- Slide 2: Why inference economics matter
  - Note: show simple per-token math and 3 levers we control: batching, caching, quantization
- Slide 3: Deployment options and control tradeoffs
  - Note: visual of Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private with pick list of typical buyer requirements per option
- Slide 4: Reliability and fallback story
  - Note: show circuit-breaker + model-variant fallback example and SLOs (p95 latency target, p99 fallbacks)
- Slide 5: Pricing and pilot options (use the templates above)
- Slide 6: Security and compliance snapshot (KMS support, audit logs, SOC-type evidence list)
- Slide 7: Customer case snapshot (see one-page case study below)
- Slide 8: Next steps and decision checklist

5) One-page case study: FinServe Retailer (anonymized)

- Challenge: FinServe needed production chat summarization and financial FAQ generation while keeping customer PII and audit trails in an approved environment.
- Engagement: 8-week Private-proof pilot, 2 models evaluated, KMS onboarding, 1-week canary on dedicated pool.
- Outcome: 35% reduction in per-request latency via batching and model routing, 28% unit cost reduction after caching and quantization tuning, 0 production incidents in 3 months post-rollout.
- Value signals to present to prospects: latency percentiles, cost delta vs incumbent, compliance evidence assembled for procurement.

6) Security FAQ for prospect DRI (targeted, concise answers)

Q: What deployment modes preserve customer data in our environment?
A: Private deployment (VPC or on-prem) keeps customer data inside the customer network. The private control plane is configured to avoid routing data through Redwood-hosted compute when requested.

Q: How do you manage keys and encryption?
A: Redwood integrates with customer KMS and HSM providers using envelope encryption. Keys can be customer-managed; audit trails show key usage events.

Q: What audit and trace data do you provide for model invocations?
A: We provide token-level tracing, per-request metadata (route, model version, latency), and configurable retention windows. Audit logs are exportable to the customer SIEM.

Q: Do you allow model weights to be run only on customer infrastructure?
A: Yes. Our on-prem package enables running model weights within customer-controlled hardware with optional air-gap installation and offline attestation steps.

Q: How do you prevent data leakage across tenants?
A: Tenant isolation is enforced at the runtime and orchestration layer: dedicated pools and strict KV cache scoping. Access control and network segmentation are standard in dedicated and private modes.

Q: What compliance artifacts can you provide during procurement?
A: SOC-type reports, penetration test summaries, data flow diagrams, and a security onboarding checklist. Specific artifacts vary by region and contract scope.

7) Pilot success metrics and go/no-go checklist

Minimum success metrics to propose up front (choose 4 for every pilot):
- Latency: p95 under target threshold for the route (example: p95 < 250 ms for UI use cases)
- Cost: per-request unit cost within X% of budgeted baseline after optimization steps (example: within 20%)
- Quality: minimum NPS or accuracy threshold on a curated prompt set (example: > 92% match to golden responses on 50 prompts)
- Reliability: zero P1 incidents during the operational canary window and error rate below 0.5%

Go/no-go decision checklist (1 line each):
1) Integration complexity acceptable to engineering stakeholders
2) Security evidence meets procurement needs or clear remediation plan exists
3) Economics show a path to desired unit cost at scale
4) Internal champion and handoff plan to ops exist

8) Operational handoff and escalation

- Primary Redwood contact for pilots: Solutions Engineer assigned per account (include contact card in pitch materials).
- Typical handoff timeline to customer ops: 2-week runbook transfer, runbook includes monitoring queries, rollback steps, and incident contact list.

9) Appendix and quick references

- Short TCO formula to share with finance teams:
  - Estimated monthly cost = (avg tokens per request * requests per month * token price) - expected savings from caching and batching (estimated percent) + reserved capacity fees if applicable

- Sample CLI snippet to run a quick latency test against hosted API (redwoodctl is used as an example):
  - redwoodctl invoke --model rdx-llama-2-13b --prompt-file sample_prompts.json --concurrency 8 --measure p95,p99

- Links to internal artifacts to attach to pitch: solution architecture diagrams, SOC evidence pack template, dedicated capacity SLA summary, price model worksheets.
